title: At the Airport
speaker: BBC Learning English
description: Essential vocabulary and phrases for navigating an airport — check-in, security, gates, and boarding.
summary:
This BBC Learning English lesson covers all the essential *vocabulary* and *phrases* you need at an international airport. The video walks through a complete airport journey from arrival at the terminal to boarding the plane.

At *check-in*, travellers need to know how to ask about their *seat assignment*, whether they have *checked baggage* or just *carry-on luggage*, and how to get their *boarding pass*. Key phrases include: 'I'd like a window seat, please', 'How many bags can I check?', and 'Is my flight on time?'

Passing through *security* requires specific vocabulary: *metal detector*, *X-ray machine*, *remove your shoes*, *liquids bag*, and *prohibited items*. The lesson explains what passengers must do at each checkpoint and the commands security officers commonly use.

Once through security, travellers head to the *departure lounge* to find their *gate*. The video explains how to read *flight information boards*, understand *departure* and *arrival* times, and what the difference is between *direct* and *connecting* flights. Common announcements heard over the PA system are introduced, such as 'Now boarding rows 20 to 30' and 'Final call for passengers on flight BA204'.

The lesson also covers *duty-free* shopping, finding *airport facilities* like restaurants and lounges, and asking for directions inside a large terminal. Useful expressions include: 'Where is gate 14?', 'How long is the walk?', and 'Is there a currency exchange here?'

On the plane, learners meet vocabulary for *overhead lockers*, *tray tables*, *seatbelts*, *emergency exits*, and *in-flight entertainment*. Standard announcements from *flight attendants* are presented in full, including the safety demonstration and instructions for landing.

Throughout the video, key vocabulary items are highlighted on screen and repeated in natural conversation, helping learners recognise words both when spoken quickly and when read on signs. The lesson targets A2–B1 level learners and uses clear, slow speech ideal for classroom comprehension activities.

title: Learn English for Hotel and Tourism: Checking Into a Hotel
speaker: LinguaTV
description: A realistic hotel check-in dialogue with key vocabulary and phrases for guests and hospitality staff.
summary:
This LinguaTV lesson uses a realistic hotel scenario to teach the vocabulary and phrases needed to check into a hotel confidently in English. The video presents a complete check-in conversation between a guest and a receptionist, making it useful both for travellers and for students working in hospitality.

At *reception*, the conversation covers standard check-in steps: confirming a *reservation*, presenting identification, specifying room preferences (*non-smoking*, *high floor*, *king bed* or *twin beds*), and receiving the *room key card*. Key guest phrases include 'I have a reservation under the name...', 'Is breakfast included in the rate?', and 'Could I have a room away from the lift?'

The receptionist's side of the dialogue is presented clearly, including common questions guests will be asked: 'Could I see your passport or ID?', 'How will you be paying?', 'Would you like help with your luggage?' Learners hear both formal and natural spoken English, including contracted forms and polite intonation.

Vocabulary for *hotel facilities* is introduced in context: *gym*, *spa*, *swimming pool*, *room service*, *concierge*, *business centre*, and *laundry service*. The lesson explains how to ask about these amenities and the hours they operate.

The video also models common *requests during a stay*: asking for extra *towels*, reporting a problem with the *air conditioning* or *Wi-Fi*, and requesting a *wake-up call* or *late checkout*. Polite request structures — 'Could you...', 'I was wondering if...', 'Would it be possible to...' — are demonstrated in natural speech.

Checkout language is briefly covered: requesting the *bill*, querying *charges*, and asking for a *receipt*. The lesson targets A2–B1 learners and suits both general travel English preparation and vocational hospitality training.

title: Ordering Food at a Restaurant
speaker: Oxford Online English
description: A complete guide to dining out in English — from reading the menu to paying the bill.
summary:
This Oxford Online English lesson covers everything you need to have a confident dining experience in an English-speaking restaurant. The video follows a complete restaurant visit and explains the vocabulary and phrases for each stage.

When you arrive, a *host* or *hostess* asks 'Do you have a *reservation*?' or 'How many in your party?' Learners practise asking for a *table for two*, requesting a specific spot ('Could we sit by the window?'), and understanding responses when the restaurant is full.

Studying the *menu* requires specific vocabulary: *starters* (or *appetisers*), *main courses* (or *entrées*), *sides*, *desserts*, and *beverages*. The lesson explains common *cooking methods* — *grilled*, *fried*, *baked*, *steamed*, *roasted* — and *dietary terms* like *vegetarian*, *vegan*, *gluten-free*, and *dairy-free*.

When the *waiter* or *waitress* comes to take your *order*, key phrases include: 'I'll have the pasta, please', 'What do you recommend?', 'Does this dish contain nuts?', and 'Could I substitute the fries for a salad?' The lesson also covers how to order *drinks* — still or sparkling water, wine by the glass or bottle, and non-alcoholic options.

During the meal, learners practise asking for *condiments* ('Could we have some ketchup?'), requesting *more bread*, and calling the waiter's attention politely ('Excuse me, could we get the bill?').

Common *problems* are addressed: a dish arriving cold, receiving the wrong order, or waiting too long. The video models polite complaint language that is firm but not rude.

Paying the *bill* involves vocabulary like *tip*, *service charge*, *split the bill*, *go Dutch*, and *receipt*. The difference between paying with *cash* and *card* is explained, and common questions like 'Is service included?' are answered.

The lesson targets A2–B1 learners with clear speech, on-screen text, and realistic conversational modelling throughout.

title: Asking for and Giving Directions
speaker: Oxford Online English
description: How to ask for directions politely and understand the instructions you receive when getting around in English.
summary:
This Oxford Online English lesson teaches the full range of language needed to ask for and give directions confidently in English. It is one of the most essential practical skills for travellers and is covered in clear, step-by-step detail.

The lesson begins with *how to ask* — using polite openings such as 'Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to...?', 'Sorry to bother you, but do you know where...?', and 'Am I going the right way to...?' The video explains why politeness markers matter in English and how native speakers might react differently to abrupt vs. polite requests.

*Prepositions of place* are introduced with visual diagrams: *next to*, *opposite*, *between*, *behind*, *in front of*, *above*, *below*, *on the corner of*, and *at the end of*. These are essential for understanding directions when someone describes a landmark's position.

*Directional verbs and phrases* are practised in context: *turn left / right*, *go straight on*, *go past*, *take the first / second turning*, *cross the road*, *go over the bridge*, *go under the underpass*, *follow the signs for*. The lesson also covers landmarks used in directions: *traffic lights*, *roundabout*, *crossroads*, *junction*, *zebra crossing*, and *bus stop*.

Distance and time expressions are introduced: *It's about five minutes' walk*, *It's just around the corner*, *You can't miss it*, *It's quite far — you might want to take the bus*. Learners practise estimating distances in both *metres* and *miles* and understanding rough time guidance.

The second half of the lesson focuses on *giving* directions clearly and helpfully. Common mistakes made by non-native speakers — vague language, missing steps, wrong prepositions — are shown and corrected.

The video uses animated maps and real street-view images to make the directions concrete, and short dialogues model natural interactions between a tourist and a local. Suitable for A2–B1 learners preparing for real-world navigation.

title: Shopping in English
speaker: BBC Learning English
description: Essential phrases for shopping abroad — asking about prices, trying things on, bargaining, and returning items.
summary:
This BBC Learning English lesson equips learners with the vocabulary and phrases needed for shopping in an English-speaking environment, covering everything from entering a shop to making a purchase and handling returns.

When a *shop assistant* approaches with 'Can I help you?', many learners freeze. The video teaches confident responses: 'I'm just browsing, thank you', 'Yes, I'm looking for...', 'Do you have this in a different size / colour?', and 'Could I try this on?' The lesson explains the difference between *browsing*, *window shopping*, and *shopping with intent*.

In a *clothing shop*, key vocabulary includes *sizes* (small, medium, large, XL; UK vs US vs European sizing), *fitting room*, *try on*, *it fits*, *it's too tight / loose / long / short*, and *alterations*. Learners practise asking if items are available in different sizes and requesting help from staff.

*Prices and payment* vocabulary is central to the lesson: *cost*, *price tag*, *discount*, *sale*, *VAT included*, *receipt*, *cash*, *contactless*, *credit card*. Useful phrases: 'How much does this cost?', 'Is this on sale?', 'Do you accept card payments?', 'Could I have a receipt, please?'

The lesson also covers *markets and bazaars* where *bargaining* or *haggling* may be acceptable. Language for negotiating price is introduced: 'What's your best price?', 'Could you do it for less?', 'I'll take it if you can do it for...'

*Returning items* requires polite but firm language: 'I'd like to return this', 'I have my receipt', 'It's faulty / the wrong size / not what I expected', 'Could I have a refund or an exchange?' The lesson explains common return policy vocabulary.

Shopping vocabulary for different contexts — supermarkets, department stores, souvenir shops — is briefly covered. The video targets A2–B1 learners and includes role-play dialogue scripts for classroom use.

title: Talking About Public Transport
speaker: BBC Learning English
description: How to talk about buses, trains, and other public transport in English — from buying tickets to describing your commute.
summary:
This BBC Learning English lesson focuses on the language used to talk about public transport — covering vocabulary for different types of transport, how to buy tickets and ask for information, and how to describe journeys and commuting habits.

The lesson introduces a wide range of *transport vocabulary*: *bus*, *coach*, *underground* (or *tube* / *metro* / *subway*), *tram*, *ferry*, *overground*, and *light rail*. Each mode of transport is described with its key associated words — for example, buses have *stops*, *routes*, and *single / return tickets*, while trains have *platforms*, *carriages*, and *seat reservations*.

Buying tickets and asking for travel information are practised in realistic dialogues. Key phrases include 'What time does the next train to Brighton leave?', 'Is there a direct service or do I need to change?', 'Which platform does it go from?', 'A return to Oxford, please', and 'Does this bus go to the city centre?'

The lesson also covers *describing how you travel* — a common topic in everyday conversation and exams. Learners practise phrases like 'I usually take the tube', 'I get the bus to work', 'I cycle when the weather is good', and 'It takes about 40 minutes door to door.' Prepositions of transport (*by bus*, *on the train*, *in a taxi*) are highlighted and practised.

Common problems on public transport are covered: *delays*, *cancellations*, *missing a connection*, and *getting on the wrong train*. Useful expressions include 'The train's been delayed by 20 minutes', 'I need to change at Victoria', and 'Can you tell me when we reach Paddington?'

The lesson uses clear speech and on-screen text, suitable for A2–B1 learners preparing to travel or live in an English-speaking environment.
